Infighting means conflict or struggle that happens inside a group — between the very members who belong to it — rather than against someone or something on the outside. The fight is not directed outward at an enemy or competitor. It is turned inward, among people who are supposed to be on the same side.

Think of a football team. Their job is to compete against other teams. But if the players start arguing bitterly with each other, scheming to get rivals on the team dropped, or sabotaging one another's chances — that internal conflict is infighting. The fight is no longer out there against opponents. It is in here, among teammates.
The key idea: it is always internal

The most important thing to understand is the word internal. Infighting can only happen within a single entity — a political party, a company, a government, a family, a movement, a military unit, or any group that is supposed to share a common goal or identity. Members who are meant to work together turn against each other instead. That is what makes infighting distinctive.

Infighting is not just one argument or a simple disagreement. It describes an ongoing, often damaging pattern of conflict from within. In practice, it can take several different forms.

It can appear as a power struggle, where members compete fiercely — and sometimes ruthlessly — for control, leadership, authority, or resources within the group. It can appear as the formation of rival factions, where the group splits into opposing camps that each push their own agenda and actively work against each other. It can appear as backstabbing and scheming, where members undermine colleagues, spread damaging rumors, or quietly sabotage each other from behind the scenes. It can appear as personal rivalries so bitter that they poison the atmosphere for everyone. And it can appear as deep disagreements over the direction, values, or strategy of the group — conflicts so intense that they tear the group apart from the inside.

Infighting can be loud and visible, playing out in public arguments and open accusations, or it can be quiet and hidden, unfolding in whisper campaigns, leaked information, secret alliances, and closed-door scheming. Both are still infighting, because both are internal and both are harmful.
Where you will encounter this word

Infighting is a very common word in politics, journalism, business, and history, and once you know it, you will notice it everywhere. A few natural examples:

"Infighting within the party prevented them from agreeing on a leader." Here, politicians from the same party are battling each other.

"The infighting between departments is slowing down every major project." Here, teams within the same company are in conflict.

"Decades of infighting left the movement too divided to make progress." Here, activists within the same movement worked against each other instead of toward their shared goal.

"Family infighting over the inheritance destroyed relationships that had lasted for decades." Here, relatives — people in the same family — tore themselves apart over competing interests.

In every example, the conflict is within the named group. That is the defining feature. Infighting cannot refer to conflict between two entirely separate groups. It only refers to conflict within one.

Infighting carries a strongly negative meaning. When someone uses this word to describe a group, they are implying that the group's energy and attention are being wasted on internal battles rather than on shared goals; that the group is weakening and damaging itself from within; that the conflict is disruptive, selfish, and often petty; and that the group is less effective, less united, and less capable because of it. You would essentially never use infighting to describe something positive or healthy. It almost always signals dysfunction.
The difference between infighting and ordinary disagreement

This distinction is important. Not all internal disagreement counts as infighting. Healthy groups disagree, debate, and challenge each other's ideas all the time. That kind of friction can actually make groups stronger and sharper. Infighting is something different and darker.

Infighting implies that the conflict has become destructive rather than constructive, personal rather than principled, persistent rather than a one-time dispute, and damaging to the group's unity, reputation, or ability to function. When internal disagreement crosses a line and starts tearing a group apart, undermining trust between members, derailing the group's goals, or turning people into enemies — that is when the right word becomes infighting.
How it behaves as a noun (grammar)

Infighting is almost always used as an uncountable noun, meaning you do not say "an infighting" or "three infightings." Instead, you use it without an article in many cases, or alongside words like "the," "some," "much," "bitter," "constant," or "political." A few natural examples: "The infighting is getting worse." "There has been constant infighting." "Years of bitter infighting left the organization in ruins." "Political infighting paralyzed the government."

You will also sometimes hear "internal infighting," which is technically a little redundant — since infighting is by definition internal — but it is a common and widely accepted phrase used for emphasis.
Words that commonly appear alongside infighting

Certain words pair with infighting so often that knowing them will help you understand and use the word more naturally. "Bitter infighting" emphasizes how hostile and intense the conflict is. "Political infighting" places it in a political context. "Constant" or "endless infighting" signals that the conflict never seems to stop. "Destructive infighting" stresses the harm it causes. "Petty infighting" describes internal quarrels that are trivial and small-minded. And phrases like "stop the infighting" or "end the infighting" are calls to bring the internal conflict to a halt.

What makes infighting such a powerful and widely used word is the idea it captures: a group defeating itself. External threats are expected — every organization, party, or team faces competition from the outside. But infighting is a self-inflicted wound. It means a group is spending its energy, time, and resources fighting the very people it depends on, which is why it so often leads to collapse, failure, or decline. History is full of political movements, companies, and empires brought down not by outside forces, but by the infighting within.
